title: Where Continents Really End
question: Where does a continent actually stop under the sea?
hook: The beach is not the edge of a continent: its crust keeps going under the water before it meets the ocean's crust.
idea: A continent's true edge is a submerged margin of shelf, slope and rise, and whether it sits at a plate boundary decides how narrow and steep it is.

beats.prompt: Put these parts of the seafloor in order, heading out from the coast.
beats.explain: The flat shelf ends at the shelf break, where the slope begins; at the slope's base the seafloor levels out into the rise, the outermost zone of the margin.

beats.prompt: Sort each into the type of margin it belongs to.
items: East Coast of the United States
Narrow, with steep descents into trenches
beats.explain: Active margins sit at plate boundaries, so they are narrow, steep and shaken by tectonic activity; passive margins lie away from boundaries, are wide and gentle, and collect thick sediment.

beats.prompt: A river carries sand and clay worn off the land out to the sea. Where does most of that sediment end up?

choices.label: Carried out to the mid-ocean ridges
choices.feedback: Ridges are far out in the ocean; most sediment never travels that far from the river mouth.

choices.label: Spread evenly over the deep-ocean basins
choices.feedback: It sounds fair to spread it everywhere, but most of it settles close to the continent.

choices.label: Dissolved away in the seawater
choices.feedback: Sand and clay are solid particles; they settle out rather than dissolving.

beats.explain: Of all the sediment in a stream's load, 80% is trapped and spread across continental margins.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning about a convergent margin is wrong. Which?
steps: An oceanic plate meets a continental plate.
The denser oceanic crust sinks beneath the less dense continental crust.
This meeting point is far from any plate boundary, so the coast stays quiet.
The margin there is narrow and drops steeply into a trench.
beats.explain: Convergent margins are active margins, which sit at plate boundaries and are places of high tectonic activity with volcanoes and earthquakes.
